claims.text: Simultaneous wear and corrosion resistance in CoCrFeMnNi is governed by rapid, cyclic re-passivation of the mechanically disrupted surface.
Dynamic regeneration of the passive oxide film during sliding counteracts mechanical wear.
Dynamic regeneration of the passive oxide film during sliding counteracts chemical attack.
The initial CoCrFeMnNi surface has an established equilibrium passive oxide film under static conditions.
A dynamic passive oxide film forms and rapidly regenerates at the sliding interface during wear.
Mechanical sliding intermittently breaks the passive film.
The inherent re-passivation kinetics of CoCrFeMnNi rapidly rebuild the disrupted oxide layer.
Rebuilding the passive layer limits overall material degradation during tribocorrosion.
Repeated film rupture and reformation will produce cyclic variations in electrochemical impedance.
Combined tribocorrosion will produce less wear depth than an isolated wear test.
Combined tribocorrosion will produce lower corrosion current density than an isolated corrosion test.
If the passive film does not regenerate, degradation rates will approximate those of the isolated baseline tests.
The proposed behavior should occur under moderate sliding loads and standard corrosive conditions.
Mechanical disruption that exceeds the re-passivation rate will prevent effective passive-film regeneration.
Sufficiently aggressive corrosion will prevent effective passive-film regeneration.
Load, sliding-cycle frequency, and corrosion intensity may alter the rupture and re-passivation dynamics.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that sliding wear breaks and challenges the passive film, whereas the baseline rationale treats wear-only samples as conditions in which passive-film dynamics are not challenged by mechanical disruption. A wear-only sliding control still contains the stipulated film-breaking action, even though corrosion is absent.

The primary prediction compares combined degradation separately with wear-only and corrosion-only baselines, but the falsification rule compares combined degradation with the sum of the two singular damages. These are different benchmarks, so the stated falsification result does not directly negate the stated primary prediction.
